decks.module: Pulling out, parallel and angle parking
decks.domain: Parking and stopping: parallel, angle and hill parking, disabled parking, no-parking places and distances, emergency parking

cards.front: What must you do when you pull out from a parked or stopped position?
cards.back: When you pull out from a parked or stopped position, check your mirrors and blind spots and yield to all other traffic.

cards.front: Does signaling make other traffic yield to you as you pull out of a parking spot?
cards.back: Pulling out of a parking spot, you yield to all other traffic; traffic does not have to yield to you because you signaled.

cards.front: Which way should your vehicle face when you parallel park?
cards.back: When parallel parking, face the same direction that traffic moves in that lane.

cards.front: How close to the curb must you parallel park, and what if there is no curb?
cards.back: Park parallel to the curb and no more than twelve inches from it, or if there is no curb, as close as you can to the edge of the shoulder.

cards.front: Is there a set distance from the shoulder edge when there is no curb?
cards.back: With a curb you stay within twelve inches of it, but with no curb you simply get as close as you can to the shoulder edge, with no set number.

cards.front: Where must your wheels be when parking spaces are marked?
cards.back: Where parking spaces are marked, your wheels must be inside the marked space.

cards.front: What are the manual's parallel parking steps?
cards.back: The manual's parallel parking steps are to pull even with the car labeled Car A, back slowly into the space while turning the wheels sharply, and then straighten the wheels.

cards.front: Where is angle parking common?
cards.back: Angle parking is common in parking lots, at shopping centers and on wide streets.

cards.front: What should drivers of large vehicles avoid when angle parking?
cards.back: When driving a large vehicle, avoid angle spaces where your vehicle would stick out and block traffic on the road.

cards.front: What may signs tell you about an angle parking area?
cards.back: Signs may show that an angle parking area is reverse angle or back-in only.

decks.domain: Parking and stopping: parallel, angle and hill parking, disabled parking, no-parking places and distances, emergency parking

cards.front: When parking on a hill, what do you do with the brake and the transmission?
cards.back: When parking on a hill, always set the parking brake, and leave a manual transmission in gear or an automatic transmission in park.

cards.front: On a hill, how does the gear choice differ between manual and automatic?
cards.back: On a hill the parking brake is always set, and the gear selection differs only by transmission: in gear for a manual, in park for an automatic.

cards.front: Why turn your front wheels when parking on a hill?
cards.back: On a hill, turn your front wheels so the vehicle would not roll downhill into traffic if the brake failed.

cards.front: Parked downhill next to a curb, which way do your front wheels turn?
cards.back: Parked downhill next to a curb, turn your front wheels toward the curb.

cards.front: Parked uphill next to a curb, which way do your front wheels turn?
cards.back: Parked uphill next to a curb, turn your front wheels toward the travel lane.

cards.front: Parked on a hill with no curb, which way do your front wheels turn?
cards.back: Parked on a hill with no curb, turn your front wheels toward the edge of the road.

cards.front: How do front wheel directions differ downhill and uphill at a curb?
cards.back: Facing downhill at a curb the front wheels point toward the curb, while facing uphill at a curb they point toward the travel lane.
cards.memory_hook: Down to curb, up to lane

cards.front: Without a curb, does the wheel direction change between uphill and downhill?
cards.back: Without a curb, the front wheels point toward the road edge whether the vehicle faces uphill or downhill.

decks.module: Disabled spaces and when rules apply
decks.domain: Parking and stopping: parallel, angle and hill parking, disabled parking, no-parking places and distances, emergency parking

cards.front: Who can get special disabled parking permits in Oregon?
cards.back: Oregon issues special parking permits to people with disabilities and to groups that transport people with disabilities.

cards.front: How may a disabled parking space be marked?
cards.back: A disabled parking space may show the disability symbol painted on the ground as well as a sign with the symbol at the front of the space.

cards.front: When may you park in a space marked for people with disabilities?
cards.back: Parking in a space marked for people with disabilities is illegal unless you have a valid disabled parking permit.

cards.front: What fines apply for parking in a disabled space without a permit?
cards.back: Parking in a disabled space without a Disabled Person Parking Permit brings fines that start at one hundred sixty-five dollars and can reach one thousand dollars, even if you park there only a few minutes.

cards.front: Do parking and stopping rules apply when you are inside the vehicle?
cards.back: Parking and stopping rules apply whether or not you are inside the vehicle.

cards.front: When do the no-stopping and no-parking places not apply?
cards.back: The no-stopping and no-parking places do not apply when your vehicle breaks down and cannot be moved out of the traffic lanes, or when the shoulder has no room for you to pull off.

cards.front: Does a quick errand excuse stopping in a no-stopping place?
cards.back: The no-stopping list is waived only for a breakdown that leaves your vehicle stuck in the lanes or with no room on the shoulder, not for a short errand.

decks.domain: Parking and stopping: parallel, angle and hill parking, disabled parking, no-parking places and distances, emergency parking

cards.front: May you stop in a traffic lane or inside an intersection?
cards.back: You may not stop or park in a traffic lane of a highway, street or road, or inside an intersection.

cards.front: What is double parking, and is it allowed?
cards.back: Double parking, which means stopping on the road side of a vehicle that is already parked, is not allowed.

cards.front: May you stop on a sidewalk, crosswalk, bike lane or tracks?
cards.back: You may not stop or park on a sidewalk, crosswalk, bicycle lane or path, or on any railroad or light rail tracks.

cards.front: Which roadway structures and highway areas ban stopping and parking?
cards.back: You may not stop or park on a bridge or overpass, in a tunnel, or between the separate roadways of a divided highway.

cards.front: When is stopping near road work not allowed?
cards.back: You may not stop or park near construction or road work where your vehicle would interfere with traffic.
cards.memory_hook: Not where you block work traffic

cards.front: Which driveway and marked areas ban stopping or parking?
cards.back: You may not stop or park in front of a public or private driveway, or anywhere that official signs, traffic control devices, diagonal stripes or other road markings forbid it.

cards.front: How far from a fire hydrant must you park?
cards.back: You may not park within ten feet of a fire hydrant.

cards.front: Does the no-parking list also ban stopping, including at hydrants?
cards.back: Every place on the no-parking list, the ten-foot fire hydrant zone included, bans stopping as well as parking.

decks.domain: Parking and stopping: parallel, angle and hill parking, disabled parking, no-parking places and distances, emergency parking

cards.front: How far from a fire station driveway must you park on each side of the street?
cards.back: You may not park within fifteen feet of a fire station driveway on the same side of the street, or within seventy-five feet of it on the opposite side.

cards.front: Which side of the street has the larger fire station distance?
cards.back: Near a fire station driveway the limit is fifteen feet on the same side of the street but seventy-five feet on the opposite side.

cards.front: How far from a crosswalk at an intersection must you park?
cards.back: You may not park within twenty feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, whether the crosswalk is marked or unmarked.

cards.front: When does the rule about parking near a traffic signal or sign apply, and at what distance?
cards.back: You may not park within fifty feet of a traffic signal or sign if your vehicle would hide it from view.

cards.front: How far from the closest rail of a crossing must a parked vehicle be?
cards.back: At a railroad or light rail crossing, keep your parked vehicle at least fifty feet from the closest rail.

cards.front: How do the two fifty-foot no-parking rules differ?
cards.back: The fifty-foot rule near a traffic signal or sign applies only when your vehicle would hide it from view, unlike the railroad crossing rule of the same distance, which always applies.

decks.domain: Parking and stopping: parallel, angle and hill parking, disabled parking, no-parking places and distances, emergency parking

cards.front: If your vehicle breaks down with no other choice, may you stop where it is normally banned?
cards.back: If your vehicle breaks down and there is no other choice, you may stop or park for a short time where it is normally banned, as long as it creates no hazard, and you turn on your hazard lights.

cards.front: When may you park on a highway shoulder?
cards.back: When needed, you may park on a highway shoulder if passing traffic still has enough room to get by.

cards.front: When must you set out warning devices for a stopped vehicle, and how far out?
cards.back: If your stopped vehicle cannot be seen from two hundred feet away in each direction, warn oncoming drivers using flags, flares, signs, signals or flaggers set out at least two hundred feet from the vehicle in both directions.

cards.front: What warning is used for any breakdown stop, and when are more devices added?
cards.back: Hazard lights are the warning for any breakdown stop, and when the vehicle cannot be seen from two hundred feet each way you add warning devices set at least two hundred feet out in both directions.

cards.front: What must you do before leaving a vehicle unattended?
cards.back: Before leaving a vehicle unattended, turn off the engine, take out the key, set the brakes and switch on the hazard lights.

cards.front: When may police have a vehicle removed, and who pays?
cards.back: A police officer may have a vehicle removed if it is parked where parking is banned or creates a hazard, and the owner pays the towing and storage costs.

cards.front: Who pays the towing and storage costs when police remove your vehicle?
cards.back: A police officer can remove a vehicle parked where parking is banned or one creating a hazard, and you are the one responsible for the towing and storage costs.

recaps.module: Pulling out, parallel and angle parking

recap_hooks.text: Pull out only after mirrors and blind spots, yielding to all traffic, and park within twelve inches of the curb facing traffic flow.
On a hill set the brake, then turn the wheels toward the curb downhill, toward the lane uphill, and toward the edge with no curb.

recaps.module: Disabled spaces and when rules apply

recap_hooks.text: Without a valid permit a disabled space is off limits, and the fines start at one hundred sixty-five dollars.
Only a breakdown that leaves you stuck excuses a no-stopping place.
Never stop in a lane, an intersection, beside a parked car or on sidewalks, bike lanes and tracks, and park at least ten feet from a hydrant.
Fifteen feet from a fire station driveway on its side, seventy-five feet across, and twenty feet from a crosswalk at an intersection.
Fifty feet from a crossing's nearest rail always, but from a signal or sign only if you would hide it.
Hazard lights for any breakdown stop, and warning devices at least two hundred feet out when the vehicle is hard to see.
Before you walk away, engine off, key out, brakes set and hazards on.
